extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of periodical essays and newspapers (18th-century literate public); general readers interested in journalism, public praise, military training, and social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative observations about composing and organizing periodical newspapers and essays—what makes news pleasant, instructive, varied, and accurately commemorated; also prescriptive suggestions for military training and for cultivating idleness. Useful for writers/editors of periodicals and essayists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper compilation requires industry and discernment
rubrics_metrics.description: The compilation of newspapers should not be left to 'narrow and mercenary minds' who are 'content to fill their paper with whatever matter, without industry to gather, or discernment to select.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should gather material with industry and exercise judgment in selection so as to both delight and instruct readers; avoid careless filling of pages for profit or expedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition; ensure variety across editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid telling the same tale repeatedly: 'The tale of the morning paper is told again in the evening, and the narratives of the evening are bought again in the morning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide fresh material or new angles between editions to prevent reader fatigue; repetition wastes readers' time and diminishes the paper's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure news coverage to sustain public interest (progressive revelation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers might 'confederate' to divide an event between morning and evening papers, so an action may be gradually discovered and 'vary a whole week with joy, anxiety, and conjecture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately schedule and vary reports (e.g., preliminary sighting, rumours, partial accounts, confirmations, human-interest details) across days to keep readers engaged; the essay provides a concrete mock schedule (Monday morning → Saturday evening) as an illustrative model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press is a powerful political engine to be understood and wisely used
rubrics_metrics.description: The Press is 'the most powerful engine that a politician can move' and 'whether it be a blessing or a curse' depends on its employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statesmen and writers should recognize the Press's civic influence and use it with care—understanding both its capacity for instruction and its potential for 'ridiculous and degrading details' or 'terrible mischiefs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Public praise and commemoration should be precise and meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: Ephemeral tokens (flowers) are inadequate recompense; monetary or clear commemorative acts better transmit merit. A monument's inscription must avoid ambiguity—e.g., clarify that 'she won her wager' to prevent later misinterpretation that 'the lady carried her horse a thousand miles' might mean the horse carried her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recording notable deeds, prefer durable, unambiguous forms of reward and description: if inscribing a pedestal, compose the wording carefully to prevent future controversy about motive or manner; include concise factual statements that disambiguate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training soldiers by graduated, realistic simulations
rubrics_metrics.description: To accustom troops to face an enemy, construct a mock fortification filled with temptations and staged stimuli (smells, sights, cooked food, pots on fires, staged prisoners) and lead soldiers repeatedly to attack it, varying the appearance and terrors until they can 'look an enemy in the face.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use progressive exposure—start with mild simulations (food scents, safe approach), then introduce louder noises and more terrifying stimuli; vary trials and adjust gradations according to troops' tolerance; practical, staged exercises are recommended over abstract exhortation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivating idleness is a gradual practice requiring initial labour
rubrics_metrics.description: True idleness ('the vis inertiae') is not immediate; one must undergo some labour first to appreciate it and then progressively lengthen idle intervals and shorten labour until 'total insensibility' is attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For those wishing to adopt idleness as a life practice: persist in gradual habituation, be wary that want (necessity) will resist idleness, and recognize that fame, love, ambition may interrupt the process; the essay frames idleness as a cultivated state rather than mere laziness.
